source.title: An Adaptive Memory Multi-Batch L-BFGS Algorithm for Neural Network Training

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied. It includes flattened tables and figure descriptions, but no apparent cutoff affecting the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: Compares training algorithms and their held-out classification performance across natural datasets, providing conceptual evidence about how optimizer choice affects generalization. It does not test the listed claim’s central random-label memorization result.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s reported final test CCR and RNK comparisons for five training methods across six datasets. The single-run training and test loss/CCR plots are described as not permitting statistically significant conclusions; cited findings from other studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks L-BFGS variants against Adam, without an SGD or momentum-SGD comparator required for V4. Its other experiments do not test any listed version. Borrowing Wilson et al.'s validation-based scheduling idea does not test or rely on their adaptive-versus-SGD generalization finding.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that adaptive memory improves L-BFGS generalization and consistency, while resetting worsens performance. Their overall generalization ordering, based on ranks, places MB-AM first, although Adam has the highest across-dataset mean CCR and much lower variability. They recommend Adam for its computational efficiency and suggest considering MB-AM when Adam's accuracy is unsatisfactory.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares adaptive-memory and resetting variants of multi-batch L-BFGS with standard multi-batch L-BFGS and Adam on six natural classification datasets; it does not use the claim’s random-label memorization setup or compare Adam with SGD.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and model setting change which optimizer has the highest mean test CCR; Adam has much lower reported variance than the L-BFGS variants across Monte Carlo simulations.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 60 simulations per dataset, Adam has the highest mean test CCR on CANCER, WAFERS and TRASH-RA; MB wins on ETCH, and MB-AM on MNIST-R and CIFAR10. Across-dataset mean CCRs are 74.3% for MB-AM, 74.1% for MB-AMR and 74.7% for Adam. Adam has substantially lower variability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested MLPs and CNNs, held-out performance of Adam versus multi-batch L-BFGS variants depends on the dataset; adaptive-memory L-BFGS improves average CCR over standard L-BFGS.

record.problems: The paper states that the training/test curves in Figures 1 and 2 show single simulations and do not permit statistically significant conclusions. The aggregate comparisons are means and standard deviations across 60 simulations, but the supplied text reports no significance tests. The study does not test the central random-label memorization claim and includes no SGD comparator for V4.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted. Training loss and single-run training/test curves in Figure 2 are described as illustrative and not statistically significant; Table 4 reports computation time rather than a claim-version outcome. Rank values were not separately rowed because final test CCR is the primary held-out measure and the paper does not frame ranks as a test-error-gap result.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond zero training error.
Matched convolutional-versus-fully-connected image comparisons and the role of local connectivity or initialization.
All stated adaptive-versus-SGD comparisons, tuning qualifications, weight-decay and switching remedies, and word-level language-model exception.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations. Batch sizes differ between optimizers here, confounding optimizer and batch effects; epoch budgets are not matched.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, underfitting, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equal-sized random removals and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The per-dataset CCR values and iteration counts match Tables 2 and 3. Remove the record's V4 limits_scope verdict: lack of an SGD comparator is an untested contrast, not evidence limiting V4. None of the benchmark rows establishes a listed claim version.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or natural-label generalization comparison.
No width sweep past the interpolation threshold.
CNNs are evaluated, but no comparison with fully connected networks on the same image tasks.
Tests Adam against multi-batch L-BFGS variants on six datasets, but does not compare SGD/momentum SGD, broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, or switching optimizers.
No sharpness or other measured generalization property.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Across the six tested datasets, comparing Adam with the paper’s multi-batch L-BFGS variants
reader_labels.reason: Results vary by dataset: Adam has the highest mean CCR in Experiments 1, 3 and 6, while MB-AM or MB is best in Experiments 2, 4 and 5; overall mean CCRs are similar (R1-R33). No SGD comparator tests V4’s stated adaptive-versus-SGD contrast.
